# Nakaishi, Nishikawa, Hukushima 2024 — Phase transition in large language models and the criticality of natural languages

**An external work (demoted from the corpus, task-019).** The paper is not about grokking but about the criticality of natural language; it is a substantive neighbour. The card is kept in full as an over-complete excerpt; the work takes no part in the corpus's indexes and counters. The convention is in `papers/README.md`, the section "External works". The original is in [`original/`](original/2406.05335.phase-transition-in-large-language-models-and-the-criticality-of-natural-languages.md); the analysis of the claims is in the neighbouring `…claims.txt`.

See also: [the global concept index](../../concepts/index.md).

**Kai Nakaishi** (RIKEN AIP; National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics), **Yoshihiko Nishikawa** (Nagoya University), **Koji Hukushima** (The University of Tokyo).

arXiv [2406.05335](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05335), June 2024, version v3 (the last of three; in it the work is renamed and restructured — versions v1 and v2 were called "Critical Phase Transition in Large Language Models"). There is no citation count for it in the corpus table. The work is in the corpus as a neighbouring branch: grokking is not analysed here, but a phase transition in a language model is measured through external statistics of the generated text. The source is the native arXiv HTML of version v3.

## Concepts covered

**[Phase transition](../../concepts/phase-transition.md)** — here it is not an image but a measured quantity. The integrated correlation $\tau$ over part-of-speech sequences grows linearly with the length of the text at $T\lesssim 1$ and levels off at a finite value at $T\gtrsim 1$; whence its divergence in the limit $N\to\infty$ and the existence of a transition at $T_{c}\approx 1$ ([`p4-1`](#p4-1), [`fig-2`](#fig-2)). It matters that the subject of the transition is not the network but the **random process it generates**: the sampling temperature plays the role of a control parameter, which the language itself does not have ([`p2-1`](#p2-1)).

**[The control parameter](../../concepts/order-parameter.md)** — the softmax temperature $T$ serves as one, and it is directly set against the physical one: the form of the expression for the probabilities corresponds to a Boltzmann distribution, but with an essential caveat — these are probabilities of tokens given a history rather than time-independent probabilities of states ([`p7-6`](#p7-6)).

**[Effective theory and statistical physics](../../concepts/effective-theory-statistical-mechanics.md)** — the whole frame of the work. Power-law behaviour (Zipf's and Heaps' laws, a power-law decay of the correlations) means criticality in statistical physics, and criticality means proximity to a transition point ([`p1-7`](#p1-7)). The work's conjecture: the random process corresponding to natural language lies **on the critical surface** separating the repetitive era from the incoherent one ([`p7-1`](#p7-1), [`fig-1`](#fig-1)).

**[The emergence of abilities](../../concepts/emergence.md)** — the critical behaviour is not built into the architecture but **arises during the training**: at $k=0$ and at 16 steps the integrated correlation barely depends on the temperature, while around $k_{c}\approx 10^{2}$ it suddenly begins to grow with the length of the sequence ([`p5-2`](#p5-2), [`fig-4`](#fig-4)). Hence the conclusion that both the criticality and the repetitive structures originate in natural language itself.

**[Progress measures](../../concepts/progress-measures.md)** — the work gives three independent observables: the integrated correlation, the power spectrum (the number of peaks) and the perplexity on the Pile dataset. They give **different** training thresholds: the criticality arises around $k\approx 10^{2}$, whereas a diverging number of peaks appears only around $k\approx 10^{3}$ ([`p5-3`](#p5-3)). The authors read this outright as the acquisition of two different structures at different eras.

**[Critical slowing down](../../concepts/edge-of-stability.md)** — a direct consequence of the power-law decay: the relaxation time to a stationary state near $T_{c}$ grows sharply ([`p4-2`](#p4-2), [`fig-15`](#fig-15)). It is checked both for a single part-of-speech label and by a principal-component analysis in the whole eighteen-dimensional space, in which one sees that near the critical point two stable states coexist ([`p10-4`](#p10-4)).

**[Spectral analysis](../../concepts/spectral-analysis-svd-esd-fve.md)** — the power spectrum of the part-of-speech sequences. At low temperatures the number of peaks grows linearly with the length of the text, that is, diverges: the repetitions are not merely present, there are **infinitely many distinct periods** of them ([`p4-6`](#p4-6), [`fig-3`](#fig-3)). This separates the observed structure from simple limit cycles and periodic Markov chains.

**[Memorisation](../../concepts/memorization-phase.md)** — the low-temperature era is precisely the regime of repetitions: the texts slide into "The number of schools in the United States\n\n…", and an analysis of individual sequences shows peaks at frequencies that are multiples of $1/p$, where $p$ is the period of the repetition ([`p10-8`](#p10-8), [`fig-17`](#fig-17)).

**[The naive minimisation of the loss](../../concepts/nlm.md)** — its relative here: the perplexity is non-monotone in the training step. Around $k=32$ the model's distribution at low temperatures concentrates on extremely simple repetitions ("\n\n\n …", "the the the …"), and the perplexity there is **higher** than under the nearly uniform distribution at the very beginning of the training ([`p6-3`](#p6-3), [`fig-6`](#fig-6)).

**[Grokking](../../concepts/grokking.md)** — there is no direct analysis of grokking in the work; the connection is indirect and therefore important for the corpus: in both cases a sharp rearrangement sets in at a particular training step and is invisible to the usual quality measures. Here the threshold is named as a number ($k_{c}\approx 10^{2}$ against $k\approx 10^{3}$ for the second structure) and measured by three independent observables.

**[Language models on real data](../../concepts/vision-real-world-data-mnist-cifar.md)** — the setting is thoroughly practical: Pythia from 160 million to 2.8 billion parameters, the Pile dataset, and also models for Chinese, French, Japanese, Korean and Spanish ([`p7-7`](#p7-7), [`p9-3`](#p9-3)). The robustness of the results is checked against the size of the model, the language and the way the text is mapped into a sequence.

It is worth saying separately what the work does **not** contain. There are no critical exponents: not one exponent apart from the measured $\eta\approx 0.2$ is estimated, no finite-size scaling is done, and no universality class is established — the authors themselves name this as a direction for further work ([`p7-2`](#p7-2)). Nor is there an explanation: it is shown that the diverging number of peaks arises from training on natural language, but which structure of the language is responsible for it is called an unclosed problem ([`p7-1`](#p7-1)).

Cards of corpus papers: [Hong & Hong 2025](../../papers/2511.12768.evidence-of-phase-transitions-in-small-transformer-based-language-models/2511.12768.evidence-of-phase-transitions-in-small-transformer-based-language-models.card.md) — the nearest work: the same external statistics of generated text as a mark of the transition, but there the control parameter is the training step and here the temperature; [Rubin et al. 2024](../../papers/2310.03789.grokking-as-a-first-order-phase-transition-in-two-layer-networks/2310.03789.grokking-as-a-first-order-phase-transition-in-two-layer-networks.card.md) — a first-order transition in weight space; [Truong et al. 2026](../../papers/2604.13123.spectral-entropy-collapse-as-a-phase-transition-in-delayed-generalisation/2604.13123.spectral-entropy-collapse-as-a-phase-transition-in-delayed-generalisation.card.md) — a control parameter measured inside the model; [Power et al. 2022](../../papers/2201.02177.grokking-generalization-beyond-overfitting-on-small-algorithmic-datasets/2201.02177.grokking-generalization-beyond-overfitting-on-small-algorithmic-datasets.card.md) — the original phenomenon of a sharp rearrangement at a particular training step; [Liu et al. 2023](../../papers/2506.21551.grokking-in-llm-pretraining-monitor-memorization-to-generalization-without-test/2506.21551.grokking-in-llm-pretraining-monitor-memorization-to-generalization-without-test.card.md) — grokking in the pre-training of language models.

## What is shown and what is conjectured

The card editor's remarks following the analysis of the claims (`…claims.txt`). The work is physical in spirit and in typesetting (a PNAS layout), 18 pages including the appendices; for the corpus it is a neighbouring branch.

**The design solves a real difficulty, and solves it elegantly.** Natural language has no controllable parameters, so its criticality cannot be checked directly ([`p2-1`](#p2-1)). A language model supplies such a parameter — the sampling temperature — while remaining a plausible model of language. That is the work's main contribution.

**The transition is established not by the appearance of curves but by a divergence.** The key is the dependence of $\tau$ on the length of the sequence: a linear growth at $T\lesssim 1$ against a saturation at $T\gtrsim 1$ ([`p4-1`](#p4-1)). Such an argument is robust to the choice of threshold and to smoothing, unlike talk of a "sharp kink".

**The nature of the low-temperature era is described more precisely than in the preceding works.** What is shown is not merely "repetitions" but a diverging number of distinct periods ([`p4-6`](#p4-6)), and this is confirmed by an analysis of individual sequences in which periods of 9, 12 and 18 are visible in different texts ([`p10-8`](#p10-8)).

**The emergence during training is the strongest part.** Both phenomena are absent at the beginning of the training and appear later ([`p5-1`](#p5-1)), and with **different** thresholds: $k_{c}\approx 10^{2}$ for the criticality and $k\approx 10^{3}$ for the complex repetitions ([`p5-3`](#p5-3)). The difference of the thresholds is a finding in its own right, not a side remark.

**The conjecture is checked by a measure accepted in the field itself.** The perplexity on the Pile is lowest exactly where predicted: at the last training step and at $T=1$ ([`p6-2`](#p6-2), [`fig-6`](#fig-6)). This ties the physical picture to the usual quality measure of a language model.

**The robustness is checked along three axes.** The size of the model (from 160 million to 2.8 billion), the language (six languages) and the way the text is mapped (part-of-speech labels against a binary marking of spaces) — the results recur everywhere ([`p8-8`](#p8-8), [`p9-3`](#p9-3), [`p9-5`](#p9-5)).

**"Criticality", however, is shown here along one axis only.** Neither critical exponents (apart from the measured $\eta\approx 0.2$), nor finite-size scaling, nor a universality class is established ([`p7-2`](#p7-2)). "Languages are critical" therefore means, for now, "near the point at which the integrated correlation diverges" rather than a complete description of the transition.

**The measure depends strongly on the choice of the pair of labels.** The main analysis is conducted for the pair (PROPN, PROPN), which gives the largest contribution ([`p3-4`](#p3-4)); the other pairs are checked in appendix D, but only eight out of the $18^{2}$ possible ones ([`p9-7`](#p9-7)).

**The threshold for the spectral peaks is chosen by hand.** A peak is counted where the prominence exceeds $0.1$ ([`p8-5`](#p8-5)); yet it is precisely the number of peaks and its divergence that is the work's second principal quantity.

**The part-of-speech tagging is a proxy, and this is admitted.** At extreme temperatures the tagger assigns labels to unnatural stretches of text ([`p8-3`](#p8-3)); the authors answer this with a check on a binary marking of spaces, but the main analysis remains on the proxy.

**The connection with natural language is shown by a coincidence of statistics rather than by a mechanism.** In appendix H the correlation, the integrated correlation, the dynamics and the spectrum for the Pile are compared — all are similar to the critical model ([`p11-2`](#p11-2)). In the language itself, however, no diverging number of peaks is observed, and the authors state this outright ([`p7-1`](#p7-1)).

**Its place in the corpus.** The work is not about grokking, but it is a substantive neighbour of it: the same idea of a sharp rearrangement setting in at a particular era of training and invisible to the usual measures. Three things are valuable: the device of taking a language model as a controllable model of language, since the language itself has no knobs; the argument through a divergence rather than through the appearance of a curve; and the difference of the two training thresholds ($10^{2}$ and $10^{3}$), which means that the model acquires two different structures separately. The price: the "criticality" is established from one observable, there are no exponents and no scaling, and the connection with language is shown by a coincidence of statistics.
